what: Essential Properties Realty Trust buys single-tenant commercial properties and leases them back to the businesses that operate from them. Its tenants are service businesses — car washes, medical and dental practices, early childhood education, quick-service restaurants, auto repair — rather than retailers selling goods.
customers: Middle-market operators of service businesses who want to free up the capital tied in their real estate. Essential buys the building, the operator keeps running the business and pays rent on a long lease.
money: Long leases, typically with annual rent increases built in and the tenant paying taxes, insurance and maintenance.
Mortgage loans made to some tenants and related income.
moat: The deliberate choice to serve service businesses is the whole strategy: a car wash, a dentist or a daycare cannot be replaced by a website, which removes the risk that has damaged every retail-focused landlord. Essential also lends to and does repeat business with the same operators as they expand, which gives it a flow of deals that do not go to auction, and it requires unit-level financial reporting from tenants, so it can see trouble coming.
risks: Debt is about $2.5B against $60.2M of cash, and growth requires continuous access to capital markets to buy more properties.
Tenants are middle-market operators rather than investment-grade corporations, so credit quality depends on Essential’s underwriting rather than on a rating agency.
The shares trade at about 22.6 times earnings and 9.6 times sales, a premium to most net lease REITs.
Rising interest rates compress the spread between what Essential pays to borrow and the yield on properties it buys, which is where its growth comes from.
Concentration in a few service categories means a problem in one of them, such as car washes, affects a meaningful share of the portfolio.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $230.2M in 2021 to $561.2M in 2025, which is unusually fast for a REIT.
Service-based tenants are structurally protected from e-commerce, which is the single biggest risk facing any other kind of retail landlord.
Free cash flow of $433.1M against a $6.1B market value supports a growing dividend.
Requiring unit-level reporting from tenants gives management information that other landlords simply do not have when underwriting.
Eighteen analysts average a $33.19 target, about 20% above the current price.
watch: The spread between the yield on newly bought properties and the cost of the capital used to buy them. A net lease REIT grows by that spread; when it closes, growth stops regardless of how good the tenants are.
view: Net lease REITs are simple machines: raise money, buy a building, lease it back to the occupant on a long lease with built-in rent increases, pocket the spread between the yield on the building and the cost of the money. The machine works as long as the spread exists. What distinguishes one from another is almost entirely the quality of the tenants and the discipline of the buying — and this is where Essential has made a genuinely good decision that is easy to overlook.

The decision is to lease to service businesses rather than retailers. A car wash, a dentist, a daycare centre, a quick-service restaurant and an auto repair shop share one property that matters more than anything on their balance sheets: you cannot order their service online. Every other net lease landlord spent the last decade explaining why their pharmacy or dollar-store tenants would survive e-commerce. Essential does not have to have that conversation. For a portfolio of long leases, where the risk you are underwriting is twenty years out, that is a structural advantage rather than a marketing line.

The second thing I like is less visible: Essential requires unit-level financial reporting from its tenants. Most landlords know their tenant’s corporate credit and nothing about whether the individual location makes money. Essential can see which stores are struggling before the rent stops arriving, which is what lets it lend to and do repeat business with growing operators rather than bidding for assets at auction. That is how it has grown revenue from $230 million to $561 million in four years without obviously overpaying.

The price reflects all of it: 22.6 times earnings is a premium to the sector, and you are paying for the quality of the strategy rather than getting it cheaply. The honest risk is not the tenants but the capital markets — this model needs continuous access to money, and $2.5 billion of debt against $60 million of cash means the growth stops the moment the spread between borrowing cost and property yield closes. Watch that spread, not the tenant list. The tenant list is the part they have already got right.
bull: Service tenants stay immune to e-commerce, unit-level underwriting keeps credit losses low, and the spread between property yields and borrowing costs stays wide enough to keep compounding.
bear: Borrowing costs rise faster than property yields, the spread closes, growth stops, and a premium multiple meets a REIT that can no longer grow its way into it.
